protocol.legal_basis: Authorisation page (p2): 'Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative. In accordance with regulation 17A of the Controlled Substances (Poisons) Regulations 2011 (the Poisons Regulations) a pharmacist is authorised to prescribe a prescription drug (not being a drug of dependence) if the pharmacist is included on the register of authorised pharmacists and the drug is prescribed in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code.'
protocol.supervision_model: Document does not use 'collaborative'/'autonomous' terminology; its own wording: an authorised pharmacist on the register of authorised pharmacists prescribing in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code (p2). Discretion clause (p5 Key points): 'When applying the information contained within this clinical practice guideline, pharmacists are advised to exercise professional discretion and judgement. The clinical practice guideline does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual, in consultation with the patient and/or their carer.' Risk status determination (p6/p7): 'There is no arbitrary scoring system ... Pharmacists must use their professional judgement to evaluate the child's risk status.'
protocol.scope_summary: SA Health (Community Pharmacy Expanded Scope of Practice Initiative) clinical practice guideline for pharmacist oral health risk assessment and application of high-strength fluoride varnish in patients aged 18 months to 17 years. Covers 'Red flag' warning signs necessitating referral to emergency medical care (immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000: difficulty swallowing or breathing), referral to a dental or medical practitioner (immediate referral same day; urgent referral within 3 days; refer when screened high/moderate risk but varnish contraindicated), concurrent referral while administering varnish (high/moderate risk, white spot or advancing decay, no dental visit in previous 12 months), key points (caries mechanism; high-strength fluoride varnish every six months; eligible patients either referred by a dental practitioner or assessed by the pharmacist at moderate/high risk; varnish contains 22.6 mg/mL (22600 ppm) fluoride ion; only registered product is Duraphat® 5% w/v sodium fluoride varnish), risk assessment and screening (18 months to 5 years — Appendix 1 plus 'lift the lip' visual screening; 6 to 17 years — Appendix 3 questionnaire), patient history, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients (CARPA), dental history, confirming management per Queensland Health Guidelines for Fluoride Varnish (QH-GDL-410:2013) and product information, contraindications and precautions, drug interactions, pregnancy and breastfeeding, topical fluoride varnish application (at-risk surfaces, twice per year), post-application advice, adverse effects, general and preventative advice (toothbrushing, toothpaste fluoride strength by age, dietary advice), patient and pharmacist resources, and Appendices 1-5 (risk assessment tools, clinical photographs, Duraphat® application procedure with age-based doses, references). 'Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.'

diagnosis_pathways.name: Oral health risk assessment, red-flag triage and fluoride varnish application

steps.description: Red-flag triage screen at presentation (p4-p5): ''Red flag' warning signs at patient presentation that necessitate referral to emergency medical care: Immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000: Difficulty swallowing or breathing.' ''Red flag' warning signs at patient presentation that necessitate referral to a dental or medical practitioner: Immediate referral (same day): Recent orofacial trauma (not yet seen by a dental and/or medical practitioner); Facial swelling or fever from an oral infection; A toothache that is getting worse, despite taking regular analgesia; Uncontrolled bleeding post extraction. Urgent referral (within 3 days): Advanced decay (discolouration and cavitation); A visible abscess; A toothache that is not impacting daily functioning and can be managed with over-the-counter analgesics; Mouth ulcerations, pigmented lesions, or abnormal appearance of tongue / palate. Refer to a dental or medical practitioner when: The patient is screened at high or moderate risk of tooth decay/poor oral health but the application of high-strength fluoride varnish is contraindicated.'

gates.criterion: No emergency sign present: no 'Difficulty swallowing or breathing' (Immediate referral to an emergency department – call 000)

No same-day sign present: no recent orofacial trauma (not yet seen by a dental and/or medical practitioner); no facial swelling or fever from an oral infection; no toothache getting worse despite regular analgesia; no uncontrolled bleeding post extraction

No within-3-days sign present: no advanced decay (discolouration and cavitation); no visible abscess; no toothache that is not impacting daily functioning and can be managed with over-the-counter analgesics; no mouth ulcerations, pigmented lesions, or abnormal appearance of tongue / palate
If screened at high or moderate risk of tooth decay/poor oral health, the application of high-strength fluoride varnish is not contraindicated

provenance.section_heading: 'Red flag' warning signs at patient presentation that necessitate referral to emergency medical care:

steps.description: Risk assessment and screening — 18 months to 5 years of age (p6-p7): risk assessment per Appendix 1; 'There is no arbitrary scoring system for risk status due to the variability of the interaction between risk factors and protective factors. Pharmacists must use their professional judgement to evaluate the child's risk status.' 'A child with no obvious clinical signs of decay, only a few moderate level risk factors and multiple protective factors may be deemed low risk.' 'If the child has at least one high risk factor, regardless of the number of protective factors, they would generally be considered at least moderate risk of tooth decay and poor oral health and fluoride application should be considered if appropriate.' Visual screening using the 'lift the lip' technique: 'The parent or caregiver should lift the upper lip of the child in front of the pharmacist so that the front teeth and gums are clearly visible to look for signs of decay (8).' 'A torch may be used ... and a piece of gauze may be used to clean visible plaque and debris off teeth for better visibility (13).' Look for: 'signs of tooth decay (white spot lesions, brown spot lesions, cavitation (holes))'; 'facial trauma (loose or broken teeth, lacerations on gums)'; 'oral infection, facial swelling/asymmetry due to spreading infection'; 'gum disease (red, swollen gums)'; 'other relevant findings including mouth ulcers and possible signs of fluorosis.' Appendix 2 provides descriptions and clinical photographs of common oral presentations.

gates.criterion: Visual 'lift the lip' screening completed with the parent/caregiver (signs of decay, facial trauma, oral infection/facial swelling, gum disease, mouth ulcers/fluorosis)
Appendix 1 risk factors and protective factors evaluated with professional judgement (no arbitrary scoring system; at least one high risk factor = at least moderate risk)

provenance.section_heading: Risk assessment and screening - 18 months to 5 years of age

steps.description: Risk assessment — 6 years to 17 years of age (p7): 'For children and adolescents aged between 6 and 17 years of age, a risk assessment questionnaire is completed with the patient and parent/caregiver. No visual screening is required, although signs of poor oral health may be easily observable, such as plaque accumulation, decay in front teeth, gingivitis or bad breath.' Risk assessment per Appendix 3; 'There is no arbitrary scoring system ... Pharmacists must use their professional judgement to evaluate the child's risk status' (low risk vs 'at least one high risk factor ... at least moderate risk'). 'As part of the risk assessment, all children and adolescents (and their parent/caregiver) should be asked about their current oral hygiene routines, including frequency of brushing, type of toothpaste (fluoride strength) and toothbrush used, and the use of any other oral hygiene aids including mouthwash and flossing.'

gates.criterion: Appendix 3 risk assessment questionnaire completed with the patient and parent/caregiver
Current oral hygiene routines asked (frequency of brushing, type of toothpaste (fluoride strength), toothbrush used, mouthwash, flossing)
Risk status evaluated with professional judgement (Appendix 3 risk factors and protective factors; at least one high risk factor = at least moderate risk)

provenance.section_heading: Risk assessment - 6 years to 17 years of age

steps.description: Patient history (p8): 'Sufficient information should be obtained from the patient and their parent/caregiver to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations. The patient history (in addition to the risk assessment questionnaire) should consider: age; pregnancy and breastfeeding status (if applicable); current medical conditions or special health care needs that may impact on oral health status and the safe use of topical fluoride: asthma (severity and current level of symptom control), history of hospitalisation for allergic reactions; current illness e.g., colds, influenza, current infection of HSV; current and recently commenced medication (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements and over-the-counter medicines); drug allergies/adverse drug events; hypersensitivity/allergic reaction to colophony (natural resin) e.g., band-aids or medical adhesives; smoking status (including vaping).' 'Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients — Consider referring to the CARPA Standard Treatment Manual for further information for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients living in rural and remote communities (13).' 'Reminder: Pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient's My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies and current medical conditions.'

gates.criterion: Sufficient information obtained from the patient and parent/caregiver to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations (all listed history items considered)
My Health Record accessed/reviewed where available (medication history, allergies, current medical conditions)

provenance.section_heading: Patient history

steps.description: Dental history (p8-p9): 'Consider the following: Does the patient have a dental practitioner / clinic that they visit routinely? When did the patient last see a dental practitioner? What was the reason e.g., emergency treatment, toothache, routine check-up? When was the last topical fluoride application? Previous adverse experiences with fluoride varnish. History of recent orofacial trauma (within the last 6 months), oral infections, toothaches or other oral pain (including use of analgesics), soft tissue pathology in or around the mouth (ulcerative gingivitis, herpetic stomatitis or aphthous ulcers). Impacts of oral health on quality of life including sleep and school attendance. Oral hygiene routines including toothbrushing frequency, use of fluoridated products (toothpaste, mouth wash). Consumption of fluoridated water.'

gates.criterion: Dental history obtained: routine dental practitioner/clinic; date and reason of last visit; last topical fluoride application and previous adverse experiences with fluoride varnish; orofacial trauma within the last 6 months, oral infections, toothaches/oral pain, soft tissue pathology; quality-of-life impacts; oral hygiene routines; consumption of fluoridated water
No professional topical fluoride treatment in the past 3 months (checked against dental history)

provenance.section_heading: Dental history

steps.description: Confirm management is appropriate (p9): 'Pharmacists should refer to the Queensland Health Guidelines for Fluoride Varnish (QH-GDL-410:2013) AND specific product information provided by the manufacturer and TGA to confirm the application of high-strength fluoride varnish is appropriate for each patient, including: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and breastfeeding (2). General information only is provided within this guideline. Where there is any doubt about the suitability of a child or adolescent, the pharmacist should not undertake the procedure and refer the patient to their preferred dental practitioner, closest public dental service or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled dental clinic. Visit SA Dental • Dental services for all kids under 18 & eligible adults to find the nearest clinic, including School Dental Service clinics (19).'

gates.criterion: Application confirmed appropriate for this patient per QH-GDL-410:2013 AND specific product information (contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and breastfeeding)
No doubt about the suitability of the child or adolescent

steps.description: Contraindications and precautions screen (p9-p10): 'Contraindications for the professional application of high-strength fluoride varnish (Duraphat® - as per the manufacturer's instructions for use) include: history of hypersensitivity/allergic reaction to colophony (natural resin) e.g., sticking plasters or medical adhesives; current systemic illness e.g., colds, influenza; severe or uncontrolled bronchial asthma; ulcerative gingivitis, stomatitis or other pathology of the soft tissues in or around the mouth e.g., herpetic stomatitis or aphthous ulcers, recent facial trauma/oral infection; previous adverse experiences or reactions to fluoride varnish (2). Additional contraindications include where the patient: has had a professional topical fluoride treatment in the past 3 months; has severe or uncontrolled bronchial asthma; has been hospitalised for any allergic reaction in the past 12 months (13).' Drug Interactions (p10): 'No other high dose fluoride products (such as fluoride gels) should be used. The presence of alcohol in the formula should be considered (2).' Pregnancy and breastfeeding (p10): 'Duraphat® contains 33.8% volume of ethanol (up to 0.2g of alcohol per dose), as such it should be avoided for patients who are pregnant or breastfeeding (2).'

gates.criterion: No history of hypersensitivity/allergic reaction to colophony (natural resin) e.g., sticking plasters or medical adhesives
No current systemic illness e.g., colds, influenza
No severe or uncontrolled bronchial asthma
No ulcerative gingivitis, stomatitis or other pathology of the soft tissues in or around the mouth e.g., herpetic stomatitis or aphthous ulcers, recent facial trauma/oral infection
No previous adverse experiences or reactions to fluoride varnish
No professional topical fluoride treatment in the past 3 months
Not hospitalised for any allergic reaction in the past 12 months
Patient is not pregnant or breastfeeding (Duraphat® contains 33.8% volume of ethanol — 'it should be avoided for patients who are pregnant or breastfeeding')
No other high dose fluoride products (such as fluoride gels) being used, and the presence of alcohol in the formula has been considered

provenance.section_heading: Contraindications and precautions

steps.description: Concurrent referral rule (p5): 'Administer fluoride varnish (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer: If the patient is screened at high or moderate risk of tooth decay/poor oral health; If the patient presents with white spot lesions or advancing decay (brown spot lesions – no cavitation evident); If the patient has not seen a dental practitioner in the previous 12 months.' Referral destinations (p9): 'their preferred dental practitioner, closest public dental service or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled dental clinic'; 'Visit SA Dental • Dental services for all kids under 18 & eligible adults to find the nearest clinic, including School Dental Service clinics (19).' Appendix 1 (p15) and Appendix 3 (p19-p20) add routine referral requirements, e.g. 'Routine referral to a dental practitioner (including public dental clinic) is required if the child has not had a dental check-up (not just emergency treatment) in the past 12 months.'

gates.criterion: Referral arranged where any concurrent-referral trigger is present (high/moderate risk screening; white spot lesions or advancing decay – brown spot lesions with no cavitation evident; not seen a dental practitioner in the previous 12 months)

Referral destination recorded (preferred dental practitioner, closest public dental service or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled dental clinic, including School Dental Service clinics)

provenance.section_heading: Administer fluoride varnish (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer:

steps.description: Topical fluoride varnish application (p5, p10-p11, p21-p22): eligibility (p5): 'Patients may either be referred by a dental practitioner (an oral health therapist, dental therapist, oral hygienist or dentist), or assessed by the pharmacist as being at moderate or high risk of tooth decay or poor oral health, to be eligible and suitable for varnish application.' 'Fluoride varnish contains 22.6 mg/mL (22600 ppm) fluoride ion suspended in an alcohol and resin base (2, 9, 10). The only fluoride varnish currently registered in Australia to prevent caries is Duraphat® 5% w/v sodium fluoride varnish (2, 10, 15).' At-risk tooth surfaces (p10): 'a tooth surface that has signs of early decay (white spot or brown spot lesions); a tooth surface directly abutting a decayed tooth surface (in between two teeth); the four front primary teeth in the upper jaw (present in children up to the age of 6-7 years); chewing (occlusal) surfaces and interproximal surfaces (in between) of permanent molars and pre-molars (if present).' Frequency (p11): 'The recommended frequency of fluoride varnish application is twice per year.' Dose (p21, as per the manufacturer's instructions for use, varies based on age and dentition type): '18 months up to 6 years dosage: 0.25ml Duraphat® (5.6mg fluoride) (primary dentition)'; '6 to 14 years dosage: 0.4ml Duraphat® (9.04mg fluoride) (mixed dentition)'; '15 to 17 years dosage: up to 0.75ml Duraphat® (16.95mg fluoride) (permanent dentition)'. 'A single use, Duraphat® Dosage Pad that indicates the amount of fluoride to be applied, or Duraphat® Varnish Single Dose (0.4ml) must be used to ensure the correct amount of varnish is dispensed and applied.' Application procedure (p21-p22, contextualised for the community pharmacy setting): explain the procedure; don appropriate PPE; position the patient ('lift the lip' technique for young children; older children sit facing the pharmacist with head tilted slightly back); dispense the correct amount for the age using a single use dosage pad or single dose pack; remove visible plaque with cotton gauze or brushing with a wet toothbrush (without toothpaste); dry teeth with cotton gauze (one quadrant at a time; isolation with finger and thumb or rolled gauze); 'Apply a thin layer of the varnish to 2-3 teeth (as required) in 1 quadrant at a time using a disposable microbrush/applicator, starting with the upper front teeth, moving to the back, then lower teeth. Do not overload the applicator and periodically check the tongue and cheeks for varnish and wipe away as required.'; for restless young children prioritise the upper front teeth; finish by checking tongue and soft tissues for residue. Note (p22): 'Duraphat is indicated as a spot application fluoride treatment for at-risk tooth surfaces. It should not be applied to the whole dentition in one session (systemic treatment) (2).'

gates.criterion: Patient assessed to be at moderate or high risk of tooth decay, or referred by a dental practitioner for the procedure

Age- and dentition-appropriate dose dispensed using a single use Duraphat® Dosage Pad or Duraphat® Varnish Single Dose (0.4ml) pack: 18 months up to 6 years 0.25ml (5.6mg fluoride); 6 to 14 years 0.4ml (9.04mg fluoride); 15 to 17 years up to 0.75ml (16.95mg fluoride)
Varnish applied as a spot application to at-risk tooth surfaces only — 'It should not be applied to the whole dentition in one session (systemic treatment)'
No professional topical fluoride treatment in the past 3 months (recommended frequency of application is twice per year)
Pre-procedure advice given (teeth may appear yellow for up to 24 hours; soft foods can be consumed after 30 minutes but harder foods cannot be chewed for at least 4 hours)

provenance.section_heading: Topical fluoride varnish application

steps.description: Post-application and general/preventative advice (p11-p12): 'Patients and parents/caregivers should be provided with post-application instructions and advice before the procedure is undertaken. The efficacy of fluoride varnish depends on the length of time it can remain undisturbed on the teeth surfaces. As such, patients should be advised to: avoid eating and drinking for at least 30 minutes after application, after which time soft food and fluids can be consumed; not chew food for at least 4 hours after application; not brush teeth for at least 4 hours after application (10).' Parents/caregivers 'should be advised that topical fluoride varnish is a preventative treatment and cannot reverse advanced tooth decay (although it may halt further development), treat dental infections or relieve dental pain.' General and preventative advice: regular check-ups with a dental practitioner; anticipatory guidance on toothbrushing, flossing and other oral hygiene aids tailored to age. Children aged 18 months to 5 years: 'children aged between 18 months and 5 years should have their teeth cleaned twice daily by a parent with a pea sized amount of toothpaste containing 500-550 ppm fluoride. A small, soft bristled toothbrush should be used and the child instructed to spit and not swallow the toothpaste and not to rinse after brushing (20, 21).' Children and adolescents aged 6 to 17 years: 'Teeth should be cleaned twice daily (or more frequently) with a soft bristled toothbrush and a toothpaste containing 1000-1500 ppm fluoride ... Toothpaste should not be swallowed, and the patient should avoid rinsing after brushing (20, 21).' 'Floss should be used to clean in between teeth.' 'Disclosure tablets may be used to demonstrate effective methods of plaque removal.' High strength fluoride products: 'Advice on the use of higher strength fluoride toothpastes and mouthwashes should be sought from a dental practitioner for patients at high risk of decay, and the use of high-concentration fluoride toothpaste must be guided by the Australian Pharmaceutical Formulary and Handbook (psa.org.au) (22).' Dietary advice (p12): 'Advise patients/carers to avoid sugary foods and drinks (e.g., especially sugars that are in sticky forms, sugary and acidic drinks, and carbohydrates as snacks between meals) that can weaken enamel, increasing the risk of tooth decay.'

gates.criterion: Post-application instructions provided before the procedure (avoid eating and drinking for at least 30 minutes; no chewing food for at least 4 hours; no brushing teeth for at least 4 hours)

Expectations advised (teeth may appear yellow for up to 24 hours; soft foods after 30 minutes; harder foods not chewed for at least 4 hours; varnish cannot reverse advanced tooth decay, treat dental infections or relieve dental pain)

Age-appropriate toothbrushing and toothpaste advice given (18 months to 5 years: twice daily, pea sized amount, 500-550 ppm fluoride, spit and not swallow, no rinsing; 6 to 17 years: twice daily or more frequently, soft bristled brush, 1000-1500 ppm fluoride, no swallowing, no rinsing, floss)
Regular dental check-ups, high-strength fluoride product advice (dental practitioner / APF-guided) and dietary advice provided

provenance.section_heading: Post application

steps.description: Adverse effects counselling and repeat interval (p11): 'Accidental ingestion of large amounts of fluoride may result in acute burning in the mouth and/or a sore tongue. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea may occur soon after ingestion (within 30 minutes) and may be accompanied by salivation, haematemesis, and epigastric cramping abdominal pain. These symptoms may persist for up to 24 hours. The manufacturer also states that: Swelling of the oral mucosa, ulcerative gingivitis and stomatitis have been observed in exceptional cases in sensitive individuals and/or individuals with a tendency to allergic reactions (especially after extensive application). Asthma attacks may occur in rare cases in people with bronchial asthma. Retching or vomiting may occur after a high dosage/extensive application in those with gastric sensitivity (2).' 'If necessary, the varnish layer can easily be removed from the mouth by brushing and rinsing (2).' 'The recommended frequency of fluoride varnish application is twice per year.' 'There is no published evidence that has found the professional application of fluoride varnish is a risk factor for enamel fluorosis in children of any age (8).'

gates.criterion: Adverse-effect warning signs explained (acute burning in the mouth and/or sore tongue; nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea within 30 minutes; symptoms may persist up to 24 hours; swelling of the oral mucosa, ulcerative gingivitis and stomatitis in sensitive individuals; asthma attacks in bronchial asthma; retching or vomiting after high dosage/extensive application with gastric sensitivity)
Patient/parent advised the varnish layer can easily be removed by brushing and rinsing if necessary
Next application scheduled per recommended frequency of twice per year (at least 3 months since last professional topical fluoride treatment)

open_questions.observed: p5: 'The only fluoride varnish currently registered in Australia to prevent caries is Duraphat® 5% w/v sodium fluoride varnish (2, 10, 15).'
open_questions.why_unclear: first_line=true for TX-1 to TX-3 rests on this exclusivity statement ('only registered product'), not on a printed first-line designation; flagged for hugh_to_confirm so local policy can confirm.

open_questions.topic: Risk-factor rows without referral statements are recorded as risk data only, not red flags
open_questions.observed: Appendix 1 rows without a printed referral note: 'Child has a bottle or sippy cup with a fluid other than water, plain milk or plain formula during the day' (Moderate); 'Snacking between meals ...' (Moderate to high). Appendix 3 rows without a referral note: 'Child/adolescent is a recent immigrant, a language other than English is primarily spoken at home, or of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander background' (Moderate); 'Child/adolescent has orthodontic or other dental appliances that may make cleaning teeth difficult' (Moderate).
open_questions.why_unclear: Only rows with printed referral statements became red flags; the remaining rows feed risk evaluation gates (professional judgement).

open_questions.topic: Gate on_fail values not printed for screening, history, advice and counselling steps
open_questions.observed: Used: STOP for the call-000 tier and for not-indicated/wrong-dose/non-spot-application treatment failures; REFER for the same-day, within-3-days, contraindication, doubt, concurrent-referral and 3-month-interval failures; 'unclear' where the document states no consequence (lift-the-lip screening completion, questionnaire completion, hygiene questions, history sufficiency, My Health Record review, destination recording, post-application and preventative advice, adverse-effects counselling, repeat scheduling).
open_questions.why_unclear: Some branch outcomes are inferred from directive wording rather than printed explicitly (rule 5).

open_questions.topic: Referral block spans pages 4-5 plus appendices (p15, p17, p19-p20)
open_questions.observed: referral.provenance uses page 4 (first page of the red-flag section); concurrent-referral triggers are on p5, the doubt rule on p9, the ulcers note on p17, and the Appendix 1/3 rows on p15 and p19-p20.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires one shared provenance object for the referral block using the first page; ranges recorded here.

open_questions.topic: Figures and clinical photographs carry content that cannot be extracted as text
open_questions.observed: Figure 1 (p7, lift-the-lip positioning), Figure 2 (p10, common areas of decay), Appendix 2 clinical photographs (p17-p18: healthy teeth and gums; white spot lesions; advancing decay; abscess; gingivitis; mouth ulcers; dental fluorosis) with descriptive text.
open_questions.why_unclear: Descriptions transcribed verbatim; the images themselves (and any lesion they depict beyond the text) are not machine-readable from the text layer.

open_questions.topic: Guideline is adapted from Queensland instruments
open_questions.observed: p14 Acknowledgements: 'consent to use the Queensland Community Pharmacy Scope of Practice Pilot Oral Health Risk Assessment and Fluoride Application – Clinical Practice Guideline v1.1 as the basis for this guideline'; p9: 'refer to the Queensland Health Guidelines for Fluoride Varnish (QH-GDL-410:2013)'; p21: application procedure 'based on the Queensland Health Fluoride Varnish Guideline (QH-GDL-410:2013) and the Remote Primary Health Care Manual – Clinical Procedure Manual'.
open_questions.why_unclear: SA instrument relies on external Queensland/NT manuals for the operative clinical detail; jurisdictional currency of those documents must be confirmed (hugh_to_confirm).

open_questions.topic: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients — CARPA referral is to a manual, not a practitioner
open_questions.observed: p8: 'Consider referring to the CARPA Standard Treatment Manual for further information for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients living in rural and remote communities (13).'
open_questions.why_unclear: Not a patient-referral trigger, so not recorded as a red flag; noted here because it directs clinical decisions to an external manual (reference 13).

open_questions.topic: Smoking and vaping status is collected but its role is not stated
open_questions.observed: p8 patient history: 'smoking status (including vaping)'.
open_questions.why_unclear: No rule, threshold or consequence is printed for smoking/vaping in this guideline (unlike the OCP protocol); captured in history gates only.

open_questions.topic: Toothpaste fluoride strengths printed as ranges with units
open_questions.observed: p12: 'toothpaste containing 500-550 ppm fluoride' (18 months to 5 years); 'a toothpaste containing 1000-1500 ppm fluoride' (6 to 17 years).
open_questions.why_unclear: Transcribed exactly as printed (no normalisation); TX-4/TX-5 strength fields carry the printed ranges.

open_questions.topic: No clinical documentation/record-keeping section in this guideline
open_questions.observed: Unlike the sibling SA protocols, this document prints no record-making, dispensing-record, My Health Record upload (only an access reminder, p8), consent or HPI-I requirements.
open_questions.why_unclear: Nothing to transcribe into pathway documentation steps; local record-keeping requirements are flagged for hugh_to_confirm rather than invented.

open_questions.topic: Alcohol content statements differ in form
open_questions.observed: p10 Drug Interactions: 'The presence of alcohol in the formula should be considered (2).'; p10 Pregnancy and breastfeeding: 'Duraphat® contains 33.8% volume of ethanol (up to 0.2g of alcohol per dose)'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Both statements recorded verbatim; whether '33.8% volume of ethanol' and 'up to 0.2g of alcohol per dose' are consistent for each dose band is a product-information question.

open_questions.topic: No action printed for a presenter outside 18 months to 17 years
open_questions.observed: 'Service restricted to patients aged 18 months to 17 years' (p3) with no referral/escalation instruction for under-18-months or over-17-year-old presenters (the usual ineligibility statement follows).
open_questions.why_unclear: PW-1-S1 has no age gate; EXC-21 records ineligibility and the open item is what happens after NOT_ELIGIBLE (hugh_to_confirm).

open_questions.topic: Adverse-effect guidance gives no escalation threshold
open_questions.observed: p11 describes ingestion symptoms ('may persist for up to 24 hours') and manufacturer warnings, plus 'If necessary, the varnish layer can easily be removed from the mouth by brushing and rinsing (2).'
open_questions.why_unclear: No 'when to seek emergency care' instruction is printed for adverse effects; RF-33/RF-34 recorded as REVIEW_GP / medium as the mildest defensible mapping, with the mapping note above.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Duraphat® dose-band boundaries: which dose applies exactly at age 6 ('18 months up to 6 years' vs '6 to 14 years') and confirmation of the 14/15 and 17-year edges against the manufacturer's instructions for use.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The printed bands overlap at 6 years; TX-1/TX-2 cannot both be right for that birthday without a local rule.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm current product information for Duraphat® (5% w/v sodium fluoride; 22.6 mg/mL / 22600 ppm fluoride ion; 33.8% volume of ethanol; 0.25ml/0.4ml/0.75ml dose volumes; single dose 0.4ml pack) against reference 2 (DURAPHAT 22,600ppmF sodium fluoride 50mg/mL varnish tube (23279), 2025).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: All dose, strength and ethanol fields come from the guideline's restatement of the manufacturer's instructions; PI changes would invalidate the treatment rows.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Local policy confirmation of first_line=true for Duraphat® (basis: 'The only fluoride varnish currently registered in Australia to prevent caries is Duraphat® 5% w/v sodium fluoride varnish' — the term 'first-line' is not printed).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: If another varnish is stocked or registered later, the exclusivity basis and first_line flags must be revisited.

hugh_to_confirm.item: How the engine should treat risk status given 'There is no arbitrary scoring system ... Pharmacists must use their professional judgement' — encode 'at least one high risk factor → at least moderate risk' as a hard rule or keep all risk gates as judgement prompts.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The only machine-usable rule is the high-risk-factor → at least moderate risk statement; everything else is judgement and must not be over-hardcoded.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Referral destination configuration: preferred dental practitioner, closest public dental service, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Community Controlled dental clinic, School Dental Service clinics, Adelaide Dental Hospital (1300 008 222) — names, addresses, hours, after-hours pathways.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Only roles and one phone number are printed; the engine needs concrete destinations per region.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Local emergency pathway for the call-000 tier ('Difficulty swallowing or breathing') — ambulance activation, nearest ED, and how the same-day dental/medical referrals are executed after hours.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: No local escalation procedure, ED list or after-hours arrangement is printed.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Currency of the external clinical authorities the guideline delegates to: Queensland Health Guidelines for Fluoride Varnish (QH-GDL-410:2013), QH-GDL-411:2013, CARPA Standard Treatment Manual (8th ed), Primary Clinical Care Manual 11th edition 2022, and the Queensland pilot CPG v1.1 on which this SA guideline is based.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: SA operative detail (procedure, contraindications) is sourced from Queensland/NT documents whose versions must be verified as current for SA practice.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Documentation, consent and record-keeping requirements for the procedure in children (parent/caregiver consent, clinical record of risk assessment, dose applied, batch/lot, adverse events) — this guideline prints none.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: No record or consent section exists in this document; local requirements must be defined before go-live rather than assumed.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Equipment, infection-control and supply list (Appendix 4: hand sanitiser, dosage pad, cotton gauze, disposable microbrush/applicator, gloves, protective eyewear, single use surgical mask, apron (optional), single use bib, clean dry toothbrush) — procurement and local IPC policy alignment.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Equipment is printed but local IPC standards, stock lines and single-use requirements are not.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Frequency enforcement: 'twice per year' application and the 'professional topical fluoride treatment in the past 3 months' contraindication — how the interval is tracked (dispensing system, clinical record, My Health Record).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The rules exist but no tracking mechanism or source of truth for 'last application' is printed.

hugh_to_confirm.item: My Health Record access during consultations (p8 reminder) — access arrangements, consent handling and what is uploaded, if anything, for this service.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The document mentions access only; unlike the OCP protocol it prescribes no upload requirement.

hugh_to_confirm.item: High-strength fluoride toothpaste and mouthwash advice: which products are stocked/advised and confirmation that advice 'must be guided by the Australian Pharmaceutical Formulary and Handbook (psa.org.au)'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Products and strengths are delegated to the APF and a dental practitioner; local advice sheets must be prepared.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Treatment of presenters outside 18 months to 17 years after NOT_ELIGIBLE (no action printed) and handling of the 18-month boundary in practice.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: No escalation instruction is printed for out-of-band ages; local policy must define the pathway (usual pharmacy care statement only).

hugh_to_confirm.item: Pregnancy/breastfeeding pathway: Duraphat® 'should be avoided' due to ethanol — where those patients are referred and whether any alternative is offered under this service.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Avoidance is printed but no alternative arrangement or referral destination is stated.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Adverse-effect escalation thresholds: when acute burning, nausea/vomiting/diarrhoea after ingestion, asthma attacks, or swelling/ulcerative gingivitis require medical review versus simple varnish removal by brushing and rinsing.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Symptoms are described with no care-escalation instruction; RF-33/RF-34 severity mapping (medium) needs local confirmation.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Encoding of the Appendix 1/Appendix 3 'Moderate to high' risk rows and the conditional referral rules ('required if ... not had a dental check-up in the past 12 months') as engine conditions, including table-layout verification against the PDF.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Combined risk-level labels and interleaved table extraction need visual verification before the rules are trusted.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Written patient/caregiver resources for post-application advice (30-minute/4-hour rules, yellow tint), anticipatory guidance and dietary advice — which SA Health/ADA resources to supply (references 1, 5, 12, 23 listed as patient resources).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The guideline requires advice be given but does not prescribe a handout; local materials must be selected.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Pharmacist training/competency expectation for the procedure (PPE, lift-the-lip screening, varnish application) — the document relies on the register-of-authorised-pharmacists basis and professional judgement, with no separate training appendix for this skill.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Unlike the OCP protocol (Appendix 1 training), no competency program is listed for oral health assessment/varnish application.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Operational compliance evidence for each prescribing event: pharmacist 'included on the register of authorised pharmacists' and prescribing 'in accordance with the Community Pharmacist Prescribing Code' (regulation 17A, Controlled Substances (Poisons) Regulations 2011).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Legal basis is stated but the record-keeping/verification steps are not; local process must be confirmed before go-live.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm instrument version/date against the controlled copy — cover and footers print 'Version 1.0 September 2025' consistently across p1-p24.
